slides.0.title: Course Introduction
slides.0.content:
To the southeast of Anjou flows a tributary from south to north into the Loire River — the Layon. In autumn it brings regular morning mists, creating the greatest botrytis sweet wine cradle in western France. From entry-level Coteaux du Layon to the prestigious Quarts de Chaume Grand Cru, the entire sweet wine pyramid is built upon Chenin Blanc + Botrytis cinerea + a mixed terroir of Tuffeau and schist.

Course Learning Objectives

🍄 Botrytis cinerea Mechanism

Understand how noble rot penetrates grape skins, concentrates sugars and acidity, and generates glycerol and unique flavor compounds

🏔️ Layon Sweet Wine Pyramid

The hierarchical logic from Coteaux du Layon → Coteaux du Layon Villages → Bonnezeaux → Quarts de Chaume GC

🌫️ Microclimate Conditions

Master the "golden botrytis conditions" of morning mist + afternoon drying in the Layon Valley

🏆 Quarts de Chaume Grand Cru

Learn about Loire's only Grand Cru AOC (recognized in 2011) and its strict regulations
slides.1.title: The Layon Valley — Western France's Noble Rot Paradise
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Morning Mist Induces Botrytis
slides.1.highlights.0.content: The narrow, east-west Layon Valley generates dense autumn morning mist (high humidity)
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Afternoon Drying
slides.1.highlights.1.content: After the mist clears, south-facing slopes receive full sun, inhibiting harmful grey rot while promoting healthy noble rot development
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Schist Terroir
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Anjou Noir black schist + tuffeau gives sweet wines mineral tension, avoiding an overly cloying character
slides.1.content:
The Layon River is a left bank tributary of the Loire, flowing north from Vihiers to Chalonnes-sur-Loire over approximately 90 km. Vineyards are mainly on south-facing slopes on the valley's north bank — this unique topography allows morning mist to accumulate and then fully disperse in the afternoon, which are precisely the golden conditions for noble rot.

🌫️ Three Requirements for Noble Rot Golden Conditions

  1. Morning high humidity: Water vapor from the Layon River's surface evaporates before sunrise, accumulating at the slope's base to create dense mist. Fog humidity 90%+ provides the moisture for Botrytis cinerea spores to germinate
  2. Afternoon high temperature and dryness: By 10–11 AM the mist clears, and south-facing slopes rapidly warm to 20°C+. Dry conditions inhibit Botrytis from converting from "noble rot" to "grey rot"
  3. Multiple successive pickings (Tries Successives): Grapes don't all become botrytised at the same time — harvest workers must return to the same vineyard multiple times, selecting only bunches or individual grapes that have reached "pourriture noble" condition

🪨 Layon Soils

Unlike the pure Tuffeau of Vouvray, Layon lies in the Anjou Noir (Black Anjou) zone:

  • Schist: Primary bedrock, dark gray, friable, rich in organic matter
  • Tuffeau tuffstone: Marginal zones, similar to Vouvray
  • Sandy soils: River terrace deposits, excellent drainage

Key role of schist: retains high acidity and gives flint/graphite mineral texture, balancing the sweetness from Botrytis.
slides.1.quiz.question: What is the key microclimate for noble rot development in the Layon Valley?
slides.1.quiz.options.1: Morning high humidity, afternoon drying — a daily temperature cycle
slides.1.quiz.explanation: Botrytis cinerea requires a "wet → dry → wet → dry" cycle. The Layon Valley's narrow, east-west topography allows dense morning mist each autumn (high humidity induces spore germination), followed by afternoon mist dispersal and drying (inhibiting harmful grey rot and concentrating the grapes). This daily rhythm is more critical than simple high humidity — if it stays humid all day, the grapes will simply rot.
slides.3.title: The Layon Sweet Wine Pyramid
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Quarts de Chaume Grand Cru
slides.3.highlights.0.content: Loire's only Grand Cru, recognized in 2011, 34 ha
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Bonnezeaux
slides.3.highlights.1.content: Single Cru AOC, 77 ha, a historic vineyard on equal footing with Quarts de Chaume
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Coteaux du Layon (Villages)
slides.3.highlights.2.content: 7 designated villages: Beaulieu, Faye, Rablay, Rochefort, Saint-Aubin, Saint-Lambert, Chaume
slides.3.content:
Layon's sweet wine system is one of France's most complex sweet wine classifications, with 4 main tiers from entry-level to top, each with progressively higher minimum residual sugar, lower yield limits, and higher grape maturity requirements.

🥇 Quarts de Chaume Grand Cru (Loire's only GC)

  • Area: ~34 ha, in the village of Rochefort-sur-Loire
  • Yield limit: 20 hL/ha (strictest)
  • Minimum residual sugar: 110 g/L (Botrytis must be highly infected)
  • Harvest: Mandatory multiple hand picking tries (minimum 3 passes)
  • Key producers: Château Bellerive (Florent Baumard), Château Pierre-Bise, Domaine des Baumard
  • History: The name derives from a 15th-century feudal tax story about "the best quarter"

🥈 Bonnezeaux (Single Cru AOC)

  • Area: ~77 ha, in the village of Thouarcé
  • Yield limit: 25 hL/ha
  • Minimum residual sugar: 51 g/L (Moelleux level and above)
  • Three slopes: La Montagne, Beauregard, Les Melleresses
  • Key producers: Château de Fesles, Domaine Petit Val, Domaine des Petits Quarts

🥉 Coteaux du Layon Villages (7 designated villages)

  • Area: ~200 ha
  • Yield limit: 30 hL/ha
  • Minimum residual sugar: 34 g/L
  • 7 villages: Beaulieu-sur-Layon, Faye-d'Anjou, Rablay-sur-Layon, Rochefort-sur-Loire, Saint-Aubin-de-Luigné, Saint-Lambert-du-Lattay, Chaume Premier Cru (top village, upgraded 2011)

📦 Coteaux du Layon (Base AOC)

  • Area: ~1,400 ha, spanning 27 villages
  • Yield limit: 35 hL/ha
  • Minimum residual sugar: 34 g/L (Demi-sec and above)
  • Position: Entry-level botrytis wines offering excellent value
slides.3.quiz.question: What is Quarts de Chaume Grand Cru's special status in Loire?
slides.3.quiz.options.1: Loire's only Grand Cru AOC (recognized in 2011)
slides.3.quiz.explanation: In 2011, Quarts de Chaume was elevated from a regular AOC to become the Loire Valley's only "Grand Cru" AOC — France's third formal Grand Cru system after Alsace Grand Cru and Bourgogne Grand Cru. This 34-hectare zone sits within the natural protected topography of a Layon tributary, where autumn botrytis conditions are exceptionally consistent.
slides.4.title: Botrytis cinerea — The Chemical Magic of Noble Rot
slides.4.highlights.0.title: Hyphae Penetrate Skin
slides.4.highlights.0.content: Penetrates through stomata without rupturing the skin surface, creating a "micro-pore effect"
slides.4.highlights.1.title: Water Evaporation
slides.4.highlights.1.content: Micro-pores allow grape water content to slowly evaporate, concentrating sugars, acidity, and flavor precursors 2–3 times
slides.4.highlights.2.title: Glycerol + Flavor Compounds
slides.4.highlights.2.content: Generates abundant glycerol (rounded mouthfeel) and sotolon (honey, curry, nutty aromas)
slides.4.content:
Botrytis cinerea is a filamentous fungus. In "bad" conditions it directly rots grapes (grey rot), causing enormous losses; but under "good" conditions (morning mist + afternoon drying), it slowly transforms grapes in its "noble rot" (pourriture noble) form, creating legendary sweet wines.

🔬 Five Stages of Noble Rot

  1. Spore attachment: Morning mist brings moisture; spores germinate on the grape skin surface
  2. Hyphal penetration: Hyphae enter through the grape's stomata (lenticels) without destroying the skin's integrity
  3. Micro-pore formation: Hyphae secrete enzymes that partially dissolve the skin, forming micro-pore channels
  4. Water evaporation: In afternoon dry conditions, grape water gradually evaporates through micro-pores, concentrating sugar from 22°Brix to 35–45°Brix
  5. Grape shriveling: Exterior turns reddish-purple and wrinkles like a raisin — called "pourri plein" (perfect noble rot)

🧪 Key Noble Rot Compounds

  • Glycerol: 5–25 g/L (regular wine has only 5–8 g/L), bringing an oily, silky mouthfeel
  • Gluconic acid: A signature by-product of botrytis, detectable in analysis to confirm noble rot infection
  • Sotolon: Key flavor compound — honey, curry, fenugreek, nuts, maple syrup aromas
  • Phenylacetaldehyde: Rose, violet floral notes
  • Sugar: 200–300+ g/L; retains high residual sugar after fermentation
slides.4.quiz.question: Which of the following does Botrytis cinerea NOT do during the noble rot process?
slides.4.quiz.options.2: Completely destroy the skin so that grape juice flows out
slides.4.quiz.explanation: Noble rot Botrytis does not destroy the overall skin structure — it only secretes enzymes to form micro-pores, allowing water to slowly evaporate. Once the skin is completely destroyed (e.g., by rain or from sticking together), it becomes the harmful "grey rot," and the entire batch of grapes must be discarded. This is why the afternoon drying conditions of the Layon are so critical: they ensure Botrytis stays in the "noble rot" stage.
slides.5.title: Level 3-3 Knowledge Test
slides.5.questions.0.question: What is the minimum residual sugar requirement for Quarts de Chaume Grand Cru?
slides.5.questions.0.explanation: Quarts de Chaume Grand Cru has a minimum residual sugar requirement of 110 g/L, the strictest sweet wine regulation in the entire Loire region — far higher than Bonnezeaux (51 g/L) and Coteaux du Layon Villages (34 g/L). The yield limit is also the strictest (20 hL/ha), ensuring grapes achieve extreme botrytis concentration.
slides.5.questions.1.question: What is the core variety for Layon sweet wines?
slides.5.questions.1.explanation: All Layon botrytis sweet wine AOCs (Coteaux du Layon, Bonnezeaux, Quarts de Chaume Grand Cru) mandate 100% Chenin Blanc. Chenin's high natural acidity (pH 3.0–3.2) maintains balance even after heavy botrytis infection, preventing the sweet wine from being overly cloying — a key reason why it ranks alongside Sémillon (Sauternes) as one of the two great botrytis varieties.
slides.5.questions.2.question: Why do Layon sweet wines generally appear lighter than Sauternes?
slides.5.questions.2.options.1: Chenin Blanc's higher natural acidity than Sémillon balances sweetness
slides.5.questions.2.explanation: The fundamental difference between Layon (Chenin) and Sauternes (Sémillon + Sauvignon) lies in varietal acidity. Chenin Blanc's pH is usually 3.0–3.2 (very high acidity), so even at 100+ g/L residual sugar it still shows tension and freshness. Sémillon's pH is usually 3.3–3.6, and combined with Sauternes' higher alcohol (13–14% vs Layon's 10–12%), the overall palate feels richer and fuller.
slides.5.questions.3.question: What is the purpose of Tries Successives (multiple successive pickings)?
slides.5.questions.3.options.1: At different times, select only the bunches or individual grapes that have reached perfect noble rot condition
slides.5.questions.3.explanation: Botrytis doesn't infect an entire vineyard simultaneously — within a single bunch, some grapes may already have reached perfect noble rot while others are uninfected or just beginning to be affected. Tries Successives requires workers to return to the vineyard multiple times (QdC GC requires at least 3 passes; some estates make 6–8 passes), picking only grapes that have reached "pourri plein" condition each time. This method has extremely high labor costs, but is the guarantee of top botrytis wine quality.
